extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students of American government and politics
extracted.subtask_short: study of political parties in the US
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter describing the place, origin, functions, and historical development of political parties in United States government (founding through Jacksonian era). Useful for learning how parties arise, why they are inevitable in the U.S. system, and how social/economic change shaped party systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand government as persons, not merely rules
rubrics_metrics.description: "the government is not a group of rules but a group of persons" — a citizen may know the written provisions of constitutions yet "not understand the government as a going concern" if he ignores the persons and informal processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that government activity is carried out by people who make informal agreements, hold conferences unknown to law, and engage in practices indispensable to governing. Evaluations of governmental functioning should attend to personal relationships, understandings, and informal procedures as much as to formal legal provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of parties (division over selection, organization, and laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The particular individuals who shall be selected... the organization of the various subdivisions... and the character of the laws the group in power shall make and enforce... inevitably... become divided into groups. Thus political parties originate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties arise from recurrent choices about personnel, institutional organization, and policy that affect private interests differently. Any analysis of party origins should trace how disputes over office-holders, organization, or law produce groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of parties to become permanent organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Each political party tends to become a permanent organization, with officers and privates standing beside and mingling with the group engaged in the governing process."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights parties' institutionalization: leaders, officers, and rank-and-file become fixtures that interact with formal government structures. Assessments of party strength or behavior should examine internal organization and permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party leaders may exercise power exceeding official officeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: "the leader of a party in a city is more powerful than the mayor"; "the chairman of a state committee controls the governor"; "the chairman of the national committee may dictate terms to the President."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should account for informal party authority and its capacity to dominate or direct formal officeholders; power often flows through party structures rather than only through formal constitutional offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intimate, indistinguishable relation between government and party
rubrics_metrics.description: "The relations between the group of men actually engaged in governing and the group of men constituting the party in power are so intimate and so subtle that no one can draw the line separating them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should not assume a clear separation between party and government; instead examine overlaps (dual office-holding, party influence on decisions) and how party activity permeates governing institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: President as the chief leader of his party
rubrics_metrics.description: "Even the chief executive of the United States is coming to be regarded as the greatest leader of his party...recent Presidents have felt justified in taking a prominent place in party councils."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating presidential behavior or party strategy, consider the President's dual constitutional and party leadership roles and how presidential engagement in party councils shapes policy and nominations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical influence of party across nominations, treaties, and lawmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Although theory prescribes formal procedures (e.g., President nominates with advice and consent), "in actual practice" nominations are made "in close consultation" with party members; treaties and laws are often settled through party networks and caucuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how party coordination shapes outcomes: nominations, treaty-making, and legislative drafting frequently occur via party consultation and caucuses rather than purely formal institutional channels. Evaluations should seek evidence of party negotiation and caucusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inevitability of parties in human government
rubrics_metrics.description: "Parties are inevitable — as inevitable as the separate groups and interests from which spring different opinions on the functions and policies of the government."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative assessments about parties should recognize their functional inevitability given divergent interests and recurring choices; proposals to eliminate parties must reckon with their social roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for party control across federal and state legislatures (divided legislative powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The legislative powers are divided between the federal Congress and the state legislatures, so that if a party has a policy that requires federal and state legislation it must be in power in both governments."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies a structural reason for strong party organization in federations: to implement coherent policies that require action at multiple levels. Case example: interstate commerce law (federal) plus supplementary state regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for coordination between executive and legislature (separation of powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The theory of the separation of executive and legislative powers serves to strengthen the political party...popular government...requires the coordination of the executive and the legislature...and it is the party system which makes it possible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because U.S. separation of powers places lawmaking and execution in different branches, parties coordinate across branches to realize voter will. Evaluations of governance should measure party capacity to produce cross-branch harmony and candidate alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many elected offices necessitate strong party organization
rubrics_metrics.description: "In almost every election there are so many different officials to be selected, that even the most intelligent citizen cannot be expected to make a wise choice...he is compelled to depend...upon the judgment of his party."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where electorates face numerous, complex choices, parties serve as heuristics and selectors of candidates. Analyses of electoral behavior should include citizens' reliance on party cues and party leaders' nominee selection processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framers' hostility to party politics and structural attempts to check them
rubrics_metrics.description: "On no matter were the framers of the federal Constitution in more complete harmony than on the undesirability of party politics...they had constantly in mind plans to break the force of majority rule."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical assessments must account for intentional constitutional design choices aimed at limiting factionalism; interpreting founders' intentions requires balancing those design aims against subsequent party development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic interests as a principal source of party antagonism
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies of the new administration (Hamilton) "speedily aroused large and important classes to opposition...based on economic interests" (taxes, bank, excises, tariffs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies material economic conflicts (taxation, banking, tariffs) as catalysts for party formation and mobilization. Evaluations of party platforms should trace underlying economic constituencies and grievances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign events and ideology can provoke domestic party divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Revolution and reactions to it divided Americans into radicals (who wanted to aid France) and conservatives (who recoiled), contributing to party formation (Federalists vs Republicans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political cleavages often form around international events and ideological responses; analyses of party development should consider the influence of foreign affairs and ideological discourse (e.g., Burke vs Paine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Party victory does not erase opposing principles; winners may adopt opponents' policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Anti-Federalists triumphed, they "were compelled to adopt" Federalist principles (e.g., Louisiana purchase stretch of Constitution, establishment of a second U.S. Bank, protective tariff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Party transitions can result in policy continuity; evaluating party platforms and outcomes should probe which institutional or policy legacies persist despite partisan change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and economic transformations reshape party coalitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The conquest and settlement of the West, transformation of slavery into a capitalistic institution, industrialization, and immigration shifted the balance of power and created new political coalitions (frontiersmen, laboring classes, slaveholders vs eastern interests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term structural changes (migration, industrialization, slavery expansion) reconfigure party bases and alignments. Historical analyses should link socioeconomic shifts to party realignment and new political movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Western political preferences: short terms, rotation in office, and populist financial policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Western settlers developed political ideas favoring "short terms and rotation in office" and measures like state banks issuing paper money to free themselves from dependence on eastern capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional economic and social conditions produce distinct party demands and programmatic preferences (administrative rotation, banking policy). Evaluations of party platforms must account for regional economic imperatives and cultural attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrialization and immigration alter suffrage and electorate composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth of manufacturing and immigration increased urban populations, and while many immigrants and factory workers were initially excluded by property qualifications, "restrictions on the suffrage began to be relaxed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in industry and demography reshape the electorate and expand franchise; analyses of party strategy should consider how expanding suffrage and new urban constituencies affect party organization and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to strong executive prerogative as basis for Whig formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Whig party name signified "opposition to high executive prerogative and approval of congressional control over the President," arising in part as reaction to Jackson's strong-executive policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Party formation can be driven by institutional/normative disputes over executive-legislative relations. Evaluations of party ideology should include stances toward institutional authority and governance norms.
